subject: How to apply both weighting and bootstrapping in SEM (for the indirect effect) using lavaan?

messages.author: 6d37bd3b53d6200d
messages.subject: How to apply both weighting and bootstrapping in SEM (for the indirect effect) using lavaan?
parts:
Hello everyone!

I am writing here because I am experiencing problems in applying both weighting and bootsrapping in Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) using Lavaan (in conjunction with the lavaan.survey package too).


So far, have tried to apply both weighting and bootsrapping in my SEM, but it does not seem to work. I can apply them separately (i.e. only weighting or only bootstrapping) but not together.



The script below is based on what I am using on my dataset, but for making it easier to receive help, the script below uses the lavaan dataset: 
A) the first one is a simple sem model,
B)In the second one I apply weighting using the svydesign() and lavaan.survey() functions
C)In the third one I try to apply both weighting and bootstrapping. To do that I add an extra step and include the as.svrepdesign() function which should allow you to do bootstrapping.

Given the different CI and p value between model A and B, the weithging seem to work. However, there is no apparent different between model B and Cm suggesting that the boostrapping did not work!

Any advice will be very welcome!

Thanks,

Mattia



library("lavaan")
library(lavaan.survey)

#####  A)     -   SEM, (NO weighting and NO bootstrapping)
model <- 'x2 ~ a*x1
y1 ~ b*x2 + c*x1
direct:= c
indirect := a*b
total := c + (a*b)'
fit <- sem(model, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
parameterEstimates(fit,standardized =TRUE)




###### B)     -   SEM + weighting (NO bootstrapping)
model <- 'x2 ~ a*x1
y1 ~ b*x2 + c*x1
direct:= c
indirect := a*b
total := c + (a*b)'
fit <- sem(model, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
#apply weights
w_design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~y2, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
#merge models
fit_w <- lavaan.survey(fit, w_design)
parameterEstimates(fit_w,standardized =TRUE)



###### C)     -  SEM + weighting + bootstrapping
model <- 'x2 ~ a*x1
y1 ~ b*x2 + c*x1
direct:= c
indirect := a*b
total := c + (a*b)'

fit <- sem(model, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
#apply weights
w_design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~y2, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
#apply bootstrapping
w_design_boot <- as.svrepdesign(w_design,type="bootstrap",replicates=10000)
#merge models
fit_w_boot <- lavaan.survey(fit, w_design_boot)
parameterEstimates(fit_w_boot,boot.ci.type="bca.simple",level=.95, standardized =TRUE)

messages.author: b8fd92e5e3662745
messages.subject: Re: How to apply both weighting and bootstrapping in SEM (for the indirect effect) using lavaan?
parts:
Define "work", or what your expectation of "work" is.

The lack of the difference between svydesign() with
linearization/Taylor series/equivalent of "robust" standard errors and
svrepdesign() is expected. They are estimating the same quantity, at
least the way this is being done in your script. If you had the
replicate weights constructed by a survey statistician that were a
part of the data set, this would account for all data-dependent
adjustments like nonresponse and calibration, and the story could have
been different. Incorporating these adjustments is the original idea
of the survey bootstraps; one of the few data sets for which I know
this was done is Pew Research Center 2013 Survey of American Jews,
http://pewrsr.ch/16IN5U4.

Taking 10,000 replicates is a bit silly if you ask me; it may somehow
boost your internal level of confidence in what you see in the output,
but all it does it it boosts the small sample biases of the bootstrap
as a method.

I am not sure BCa methodology has ever been extended to the survey
bootstraps, by the way. BCa attacks the second order properties of the
bootstrap, and in the survey world, they are determined by an
interplay of strata and clusters and weights (of which you only have
the weights though in your simple case), and the third/fourth moments
of the data by stratum. This is to say that applying the formula may
work in giving you *an* answer, in the sense of the code running and
producing a number of some kind, but what this number really means may
be anybody's telling. In particular, the acceleration constant is
frequently produced in the i.i.d. world from the jackknived
statistics, but (a) in the case of survey data, you need to jackknife
clusters as whole, (b) rescale the jackknifed values within strata,
and (c) even with the weights-only specification like yours, I am not
sure this would work *that* well. I would not expect
lavaan::parameterEstimates() to pick these up, although Yves or Dan
could tell otherwise. boot.ci.type="perc" is more defensible.

I have a deja vu that this discussion happened a few weeks ago either
here or on SEMNET, did it not?
